readerTitle: Why Amazon's meetings start in silence
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Amazon의 서술형 메모) + Brooks의 소통 경로 공식 + 가상 적용 (소프트웨어 스타트업, 물류 창고 팀)
insight: 회사가 커지면 메시지는 내가 없는 자리에서 전달되어야 한다. 그래서 글로 남기고, 이유를 붙이고, 지겨울 만큼 반복해야 한다.
misconception: 전체 회의에서 한 번 잘 발표하면 모두가 알고, 같은 뜻으로 이해한다.

sources.text: Bezos, J. (2017). 2017 Letter to Shareholders, Amazon.com (six-page memos, silent reading at the start of meetings)
Brooks, F. P. (1975). The Mythical Man-Month. Addison-Wesley. (communication paths grow as n(n−1)/2)
소프트웨어 스타트업, 물류 창고 팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 1번·5번 카드의 인용문 "We don't do PowerPoint (or any other slide-oriented) presentations at Amazon. Instead, we write narratively structured six-page memos."는 2017년 주주서한 원문과 한 글자씩 대조해 확인하세요.
Bezos가 2004년 경영진에게 슬라이드 대신 서술형 메모를 쓰라고 지시했다는 내용은 여러 언론 보도에 근거합니다. 정확한 날짜는 카드에 쓰지 않고 "in 2004"로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 1차 자료를 다시 확인하세요.
공식의 출처는 Brooks(1975)의 소프트웨어 프로젝트 논의입니다. 모든 쌍이 실제로 대화한다는 뜻이 아니라 잠재적 경로 수라는 점을 3번 카드에 밝혔습니다.

cards.title: Why Amazon's meetings start in silence
body: At many Amazon senior meetings, nobody talks at first. Everyone reads a memo of up to six pages, quietly, around the table.
Jeff Bezos described it in his 2017 shareholder letter: "We don't do PowerPoint (or any other slide-oriented) presentations at Amazon. Instead, we write narratively structured six-page memos."
It looks slow. It's a tool for a problem every growing company hits.

image.label: People reading printed memos in silence at a meeting table
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 회의 테이블에 여러 사람이 앉아 조용히 종이 문서를 읽고 있음. 꺼진 프로젝터 화면. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your company just changed direction.
body: Your software startup grew from 15 to 90 people in a year. You've decided to pause a new product and put everyone on fixing problems for your biggest customers.
How do you make sure everyone gets it?

options.text: Explain it clearly once at the all-hands meeting
options.feedback: Everyone hears your voice, which matters. But half the room is distracted, some are absent, and by next month people will retell it differently.

options.text: Write a one-page note on what changes and why, then repeat it in meetings for weeks
options.feedback: It takes more of your time, but the message stays the same each time it's passed on, and people know the reason behind it.

options.text: Brief your managers and let them pass it to their teams
options.feedback: It's efficient, but each manager tells a slightly different version. Nine managers can mean nine priorities.

cards.title: People grow by adding. Conversations grow by multiplying.
body: In 1975, Fred Brooks pointed out that the number of possible two-person links in a group is **n × (n − 1) ÷ 2**. That's every pair that could talk, not every pair that does.
Go from 10 people to 200, and the team is 20 times bigger. The possible links are about 440 times more.

breakdown.label: 10 people
breakdown.detail: Everyone can stay in the loop by talking

breakdown.label: 50 people
breakdown.detail: Hallway chat starts to miss people

breakdown.label: 200 people
breakdown.detail: No one can hear everything directly

cards.callout: Past a certain size, most people hear your message secondhand.

cards.title: Communicating at scale
body: **Communicating at scale** means building messages that travel without you. In a small team, you explain things in person and fix confusion on the spot. In a big one, your words get passed along by people you never talk to.
So the message has to hold up on its own: written down so it doesn't drift, carrying the *why* so people can make their own calls, and repeated until it sticks.

image.label: One message passing through many people, staying the same shape
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 한 사람이 든 종이 한 장이 여러 사람의 손을 거쳐 오른쪽까지 같은 모양으로 전달됨. 아래쪽에는 말풍선이 전달될수록 모양이 찌그러지는 대비 그림.

cards.title: Why Amazon writes instead of presenting.
body: In 2004, Bezos told his senior team to replace slide decks with written memos. In his 2017 letter, he explained that a good memo takes real effort, often a week or more of writing and rewriting.

Writing in full sentences forces the author to think the idea through. Bullet points can hide gaps. A memo can also be read by people who weren't in the room, and it says the same thing on the hundredth reading as on the first.

cards.title: The same drift happens on a kitchen line.
body: A restaurant owner opens a third location. She tells the head chef to cut portion sizes to keep prices steady. The chef tells the line cooks, "go a bit lighter." At the new site, a cook hears "skimp," and complaints follow.
A short written note would have fixed it: the new portion in grams, and why it changed. When people know the reason, they can handle cases the rule didn't cover.

cards.title: More messages isn't better communication.
body: If everything is sent as urgent, nothing is. Ten updates a week bury the one that matters. Pick a few messages and repeat those.
Written doesn't mean read, either. Check what people actually understood by asking them to say it back.
And writing has a cost. A six-page memo for every small decision would slow a company down. Save the heavy tools for decisions many people must carry out.

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse team.
body: You manage a 40-person warehouse team inside a large logistics company. A new rule says heavy pallets must be loaded on the bottom shelf. It applies to all three shifts, starting Monday.
How do you roll it out?

options.text: Email the new rule to the whole team
options.feedback: It's on record and quick. But many floor staff rarely read email, and a rule without a reason is easy to skip when things get busy.

options.text: Write the rule and the reason on one page, have each shift lead cover it at shift start for two weeks, then check on the floor
options.feedback: It costs some minutes each shift, but every shift hears the same version, knows why it matters, and you can see whether it's working.

options.text: Put up a poster by the loading dock
options.feedback: It's visible, but posters fade into the background within days, and no one can ask it a question.

cards.title: At scale, your message has to work without you in the room.
body: Write it down, include the why, and repeat it longer than feels necessary.
**Try it today:** pick one priority you've shared recently. Ask three people, at different levels, to explain it in their own words. Compare their answers with what you meant.
